passage: Counsellor's note. Sunaina (Class 5) came to see me on Tuesday. She said Vikas has been mocking her lunch and pushing her chair. She was not only angry. "Maybe things are bad in his house," she said, "because nobody who is happy is that mean." I said that wondering about a reason is different from excusing what he does, and she nodded slowly. She told me she felt a little sorry for him but still wanted to stay away from him. I wrote down her account and spoke to her class teacher. I will meet Vikas separately, and I will check on Sunaina again next week.

qa.q: What did Vikas do to Sunaina?
qa.a: He mocked her lunch and pushed her chair.

qa.q: What did Sunaina feel toward Vikas besides anger?
qa.a: She felt a little sorry for him, guessing things might be bad in his house, but she still wanted to stay away from him.

qa.q: What did the counsellor do next to support Sunaina?
qa.a: They wrote down her account, spoke to her class teacher, and planned to meet Vikas separately and check on Sunaina again next week.

qa.q: How might Vikas experience being called to meet the counsellor?
qa.a: He may feel called out and defensive, or he may finally have a chance to be listened to; the note does not say, only that the counsellor will see him separately.

grounding: A child wonders why the bully is mean, feels some pity, and still keeps distance and gets adult help.

passage:
At the evening tuition centre, Mohit kept kicking Omkar's chair and calling him "brain box". Omkar hated it.
One evening Omkar waited downstairs for his mother. A car pulled up, and a man leaned out and shouted at Mohit, "Useless! Late again!" Mohit's shoulders went up to his ears.
Omkar felt something unexpected: a twist of pity.
Next day, Mohit kicked his chair again. Omkar didn't kick back, but he didn't pretend it was okay either. He moved to the front row and told Mahima Ma'am, who ran the centre. She thanked him, spoke to Mohit that same evening, and changed the seating. Omkar still felt a bit sorry for Mohit. But sorry wasn't the same as fine.

qa.q: What mixed feelings did Omkar have about Mohit after seeing the man in the car?
qa.a: Omkar felt pity for Mohit, sensing he might be hurt at home, while still being upset about the chair-kicking.

qa.q: What did Omkar do that balanced understanding and safety?
qa.a: He didn't fight back, moved to the front row and told Mahima Ma'am, keeping away from Mohit without excusing him.

qa.q: How might Mahima Ma'am see the situation?
qa.a: Mahima Ma'am sees a child being bullied who needs protection, so she speaks to Mohit and changes the seating that evening.

grounding: A boy bullied at tuition glimpses the bully being shouted at by an adult and feels some pity, but still keeps away and tells the adult in charge.

passage:
Monday. A Class 6 boy called Karan kept snatching Asif's cap and throwing it on the roof shed. Asif went home fuming.
Wednesday. In the canteen, Asif saw Karan eating alone, with an old bruise on his arm and no lunch box, only a biscuit packet. Asif thought, maybe he's hurting at home. The anger went quieter.
Thursday. Karan grabbed the cap again. Asif felt sorry for him, but he still didn't want this. At break he told Vishal Sir, the PE teacher, about the cap and about the bruise. Vishal Sir thanked him and said he'd talk to Karan that day and let the counsellor know. Asif stayed near his friends. Understanding Karan didn't mean putting up with it.

qa.q: Where did Karan throw Asif's cap?
How did Asif's feelings towards Karan change on Wednesday?
qa.a: His anger quietened into pity when he saw Karan eating alone with a bruise and only a biscuit packet, and wondered if he was hurting at home.

qa.q: Why was telling Vishal Sir about both the cap and the bruise a good choice?
qa.a: It protected Asif from the bullying and also let an adult check on Karan, who might need help himself.

qa.q: How might Vishal Sir see what Asif told him?
qa.a: Vishal Sir takes both parts seriously, thanking Asif, planning to talk to Karan that day and alerting the counsellor.

grounding: A boy wonders why a bully is mean and guesses he may be hurt at home; he feels pity but still keeps away and asks adults for help.
